messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Claire Martin is a 39-year-old city council member who came to treatment after months of worsening insomnia and a growing sense that her world had narrowed to a few places where she could still breathe normally. She is married and outwardly composed in public, known for sitting through contentious council meetings with a steady face, but in the consulting room she described living as if danger could step out from almost anyone at any time. What finally pushed her to seek help was not a single new event, but the recognition that even in ordinary settings she was scanning constantly—watching hands, jaw tension, shifts in tone, the way one person moved toward another—and that she was no longer certain she could keep doing her job this way.

The experiences that organize her distress trace back to childhood, when she repeatedly witnessed violence between adults at home. Claire does not tell that history as a complete story. Instead, it comes in jagged pieces: one instant is unnervingly sharp, the next entirely absent. She can describe with striking precision the angle of a kitchen chair tipped over on linoleum and the sound of a body being shoved against a wall, yet there are stretches around those moments that disappear when she reaches for them. Some parts, she said, are “just gone,” no matter how hard she tries to recover them. What is clearest is not always visual. At times when the memory intrudes, she feels her own body lock into the same position she held as a child—shoulders pulled in, back rigid, breath shallow, as if she is again trying to become small and still enough not to be noticed.

Those fractured memories feed directly into how unsafe the present feels to her. Because the past comes back in flashes and bodily states rather than as something finished and over, Claire has come to feel that danger is difficult to predict and could emerge anywhere behind an ordinary interaction. She watches other people closely for signs they might turn harmful: a spouse cutting another off mid-sentence at a restaurant, a staff member’s voice hardening in the hallway outside her office, a man at a council meeting standing too abruptly from his seat. In those moments, what comes over her is not simply recollection but the sense that her body already knows what is about to happen. The result is that only a very small number of places feel safe—her bedroom with the door shut, her office when no one else is there, occasionally her parked car before she has to go into a building. Everywhere else requires vigilance.

That vigilance, in turn, seems to keep the old experience close to the surface. At work, where public disagreement is routine, Claire finds herself studying the room instead of hearing the full discussion, tracking who is flushed, who is clenching a fist, who is leaning too close across the dais. Later, when she lies down at night, keyed up from a day of monitoring everyone around her, the clear fragments return with force while the missing parts remain maddeningly blank. She may feel her spine press rigidly into the mattress as if bracing against a wall, her arms held tight to her sides before she even realizes why. Sleep is hard to fall into and hard to stay in. She wakes alert, listening. The more closely she has watched for threat during the day, the more vividly her body seems to re-enter those childhood moments after dark.

Over the years this has altered how she lives with her husband and how she manages the ordinary demands of public life. She prefers to meet people in controlled settings and feels markedly more at ease if she knows exactly where she can sit and how quickly she could leave. At city hall she sometimes lingers in her office rather than stepping into crowded informal conversations, telling herself she works better alone there, though privately she knows the room feels containable in a way the corridor does not. Her husband has noticed that she relaxes only in a few tightly bounded spaces and that evenings are often spent with her attention divided, one part of her following him and every nearby sound. Claire is troubled by how small that “safe zone” has become. She fears that if she keeps living this way, she will lose the ability to be fully present in the career she values and in her marriage. She has come for help because she wants, more than anything, to stop feeling as though her body is still trapped inside moments she cannot fully remember, and because she is frightened that if she does not, nowhere outside those few protected places will ever feel safe again.
